metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
Structural weight capacity, not electrical supply, is now the binding constraint in many data center retrofits for liquid-cooled AI racks.

Liquid cooling systems add coolant, manifolds, and batteries that make modern AI racks far heavier than the enterprise equipment most buildings were designed to support. Raised floors and slabs engineered decades ago for conventional servers cannot bear the load of new hardware without costly reconstruction. Retrofit projects routinely hit structural limits before they encounter power delivery constraints, reversing the historical priority of electrical infrastructure in data center planning.

This matters because it extends the timeline and cost of bringing existing facilities online for AI workloads. A building with spare electrical capacity can still be unusable if its floor cannot support the weight density required. The constraint is physical and immovable, not a matter of running more cables or upgrading substations.

The data does not address how widespread this problem is across the installed base of data centers, how much retrofit cost it adds on average, or whether new construction solves it. It captures a shift in what limits scaling, not the total impact on AI infrastructure deployment.
